details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: Is there a ceiling on any individual resource dimension — for example, a maximum energy draw of X kWh or a maximum machine speed of Y% of rated capacity — beyond which the optimizer must not go, even if fatigue and noise constraints are still satisfied? Without a cap, the optimizer may legally increase power consumption by ~40% to squeeze marginal efficiency gains.
flags.resolution: Cap machine_speed_setpoints at 100% of manufacturer-rated speed and apply no additional energy ceiling; the hard constraints on fatigue and noise are treated as the sole binding limits on resource escalation.

flags.question: Is the 0.4 fatigue threshold an instantaneous ceiling that must never be crossed at any 5-minute reading, or is it an end-of-shift cumulative limit — and if instantaneous, should the optimizer apply a tighter intra-shift budget (e.g. ≤ 0.3 for the first 6 hours) to leave headroom before the shift ends?
flags.resolution: Treat the threshold as a hard instantaneous ceiling (≤ 0.4 at every 5-minute control step) with no additional intra-shift budget reserve; the optimizer may run operators at up to 0.4 throughout the entire shift.

flags.field: resource_efficiency (multi-resource weighting: energy vs. material vs. labour)
flags.question: When trading off between resource types — for instance, running machines faster (more energy, less labour-hours) versus slower (less energy, more labour-hours) — should each resource be weighted equally in the efficiency denominator, or do you want energy, raw material, and labour to carry specific relative weights (e.g. 50%, 30%, 20%)?
flags.resolution: Normalise each resource to its shift-level budget and weight equally (1/3 each) in the composite denominator, using MES/ERP baselines as the normalisation reference.

flags.question: The 80 dB(A) limit is implemented as a 5-minute Leq (equivalent continuous level), which permits short bursts well above 80 dB provided the average stays under the limit. Should there also be a peak constraint — for example, no single instantaneous reading above 85 dB(A) — to match the EU Directive 2003/10/EC peak action level?
flags.resolution: Apply only the Leq constraint (≤ 80 dB(A) per 5-minute window) with no separate instantaneous peak limit, consistent with the stated noise_threshold_source.

flags.question: Since task rotation is a decision variable updated every 5 minutes, should a minimum continuous task duration be enforced (e.g. no rotation more frequently than every 30 minutes) to avoid disruptive micro-rotations that the fatigue sensors may not capture but that degrade skill continuity and productivity?
flags.resolution: Allow rotation at any control step (every 5 minutes) with no minimum dwell time; the optimizer may rotate freely as long as the fatigue and noise constraints are met.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The baseline demand assumption rose from 52.0 to 65.0 UPH (+25%), but schedule S1 was dimensioned for the lower target. Actual throughput (40.7 UPH) was already lagging the original plan; against the revised demand of 65.0 UPH the production shortfall is now ~37.4%. Each scheduling cycle that passes with output at 40.7 UPH accumulates a unit-deficit that the remaining Phase 2 window cannot absorb at the current pace, directly eroding the deadline margin. The negative DeadlineGap margin (-0.374) confirms the cumulative deficit has already crossed the tolerance boundary: the committed delivery volume will not be reached by the contracted deadline unless throughput is sharply increased or the deadline is renegotiated.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately escalate to the production supervisor and trigger a re-plan of schedule S1 with demand_base_uph=65. In parallel, evaluate authorising a controlled robot-speed increase to recover throughput headroom, while monitoring noise_db and energy_kwh to ensure they remain within their own constraint envelopes. If throughput cannot be raised sufficiently within the next cycle, initiate customer/logistics notification for potential deadline slip.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: r2 is running at maximum speed (1.0), making it the dominant noise contributor. Noise scales with robot speed; reducing r2 by 15% directly addresses the 4.9 dB overage. r1 at 0.9 is already modulated, so r2 is the binding knob for noise. A 0.15 reduction in the higher-speed robot yields an estimated 4–6 dB noise reduction, bringing the combined noise level to approximately 79–80 dB.

The fatigue index of 0.6001 must drop to ≤0.4 — a required reduction of >33%. Human cycle rate is the direct and primary driver of fatigue accumulation; no other parameter addresses this constraint as efficiently. Assuming approximately linear scaling (fatigue ≈ base_rate × multiplier), the current base rate implies ~0.522 per unit multiplier, so the ceiling is 0.4/0.522 ≈ 0.77. Setting 0.80 provides a small safety margin above this threshold while minimizing throughput loss.

Even after reducing the cycle rate multiplier, the fatigue index may sit close to the 0.4 boundary. Increasing buffer time from 1.0 s to 1.5 s inserts micro-recovery intervals into the pipeline, providing passive fatigue relief without further cutting throughput. This is the smallest supplemental lever that does not require additional changes to robot speed or human pace, and the 0.5 s increase has negligible impact on cycle time relative to typical operation durations.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 25% surge in production demand has produced a schedule that violates two human-centric constraints simultaneously. The Fatigue Index reached 0.6001, exceeding the hard ceiling of 0.40 by a margin of 0.2001 — a 50% overrun above the limit — while ambient Noise reached 84.9 dB against the 80.0 dB maximum, a 4.9 dB exceedance. Both violations represent legally and ergonomically significant risks to worker health and safety. The current schedule cannot be executed as generated; production manager authorization is required before any remediation path is adopted.

Option 2 — Deploy Noise Attenuation Engineering Controls and Revise Rotation Schedule
Option 3 — Temporary Dual-Constraint Relaxation with Enhanced Monitoring (Last Resort)

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with both FatigueIndex (100% violation) and Noise (80% violation) severely breached under a +25% demand surge. Prior learning shows S2 policy was rejected twice in similar situations while S3 was accepted twice, indicating the current policy family is fundamentally misaligned. MICRO parameter tweaks (±5% speed, ±10% cycle rate) are insufficient to resolve a 100% fatigue violation under a 25% demand surge — the operating regime itself is wrong. MACRO full replan is not yet warranted because prior experience demonstrates S3 resolves similar disturbances, meaning a policy family switch is the appropriate and proven remedy.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience is decisive: S2 rejected 2/2 times and S3 accepted 2/2 times in analogous situations. The fatigue constraint at 100% violation probability under sustained demand surge cannot be resolved by small parameter tweaks to the current S2 policy; switching to the S3 policy family (robust/conservative) directly addresses both the fatigue and noise constraints without requiring full L1-L2 replanning.

experience_synthesis.insight: Across both demand_surge episodes, policy S3 consistently satisfied constraints while S2 was deterministically rejected for violating both Fatigue (>0.4) and Noise (>80dB) thresholds simultaneously. S3 achieved stable throughput in the range 29.4–29.6 UPH with deadline gaps of 50.5–52.9%, suggesting it handles surge load adequately but leaves significant deadline slack—planners may explore tighter scheduling within S3. Confidence is moderate-low due to only 2 observations; the perfect consistency of outcomes raises signal strength, but the sample is too small to rule out confounding context factors.
